title: Lasagna alla Bolognese
author: Marco Bellini
desc: Lasagna alla Bolognese layers delicate green spinach pasta sheets with rich ragù and silky béchamel — the true, Bologna-born ancestor of the baked pasta dish known worldwide.
longDesc: Unlike the tomato-and-ricotta-heavy versions found abroad, authentic Bolognese lasagna uses thin sheets of fresh pasta (traditionally colored green with spinach), layered with the same slow-cooked ragù used for tagliatelle, bound together with a delicate béchamel rather than ricotta.
ingredients: 1 batch Ragù alla Bolognese (as in ITA029, doubled for layering)
12–15 sheets fresh lasagna pasta (spinach-green traditional, or plain)
Salt and white pepper, to taste
steps: Prepare the béchamel: melt the butter in a saucepan, whisk in the flour, and cook for 1–2 minutes to form a roux.
Gradually whisk in the warm milk, a little at a time, until fully smooth. Simmer, stirring constantly, for 8–10 minutes until thickened. Season with nutmeg, salt, and white pepper.
If using fresh (unbaked) pasta sheets, briefly blanch each in salted boiling water for 30 seconds, then lay flat on a towel — this step can be skipped with fresh no-boil sheets.
Spread a thin layer of ragù on the base of a baking dish, followed by a layer of pasta sheets.

Spread a layer of béchamel over the pasta, then a layer of ragù, then a scatter of Parmigiano. Repeat the layering — pasta, béchamel, ragù, cheese — until you have 5–6 layers, finishing with a generous layer of béchamel and Parmigiano on top.
Bake for 35–40 minutes until bubbling and golden on top.
Rest for 10–15 minutes before slicing — this allows the layers to set for clean portions.
chefTips: Resting the baked lasagna before cutting is essential — slicing immediately causes the layers to slide apart.
Thin, delicate pasta sheets are traditional in Bologna — thick, chewy sheets are a departure from the authentic style.
Make the ragù and béchamel a day ahead to streamline assembly day.
commonMistakes: Using ricotta instead of béchamel — this is a distinctly non-Bolognese substitution common in other regional and international styles.
Skipping the rest time after baking, resulting in a lasagna that falls apart when sliced.
Making the béchamel too thick or too thin — it should be pourable but coat the back of a spoon.
storage: Refrigerate for up to 4 days, or freeze baked or unbaked for up to 3 months.
reheating: Reheat covered in a 180°C (350°F) oven until warmed through, about 20–25 minutes from chilled.
healthBenefits: A good source of protein, calcium, and iron.
Best enjoyed as a hearty, occasional main course given its richness.
culturalNote: The oldest known lasagna recipe in Italian dates to a 14th-century manuscript, though the Bolognese ragù-and-béchamel version as known today solidified in the 19th and 20th centuries.
